mcqs.question: Checkout calls the Payments service synchronously and waits for a response before confirming the order. What is the main reason this should be synchronous rather than event-based?
options: Checkout genuinely cannot proceed until it knows whether the charge succeeded, so it needs the answer right now
Synchronous calls are always faster than asynchronous ones regardless of the workload
REST and gRPC cannot be used for anything except synchronous calls
Asynchronous calls are not possible between two services owned by different teams
mcqs.explanation: The defining test for synchronous vs asynchronous is whether the caller needs the result to take its next step — checkout can't confirm an order without knowing if the charge succeeded, so it must wait. Synchronous isn't inherently faster, both protocols can be used either way in principle, and team ownership has nothing to do with the sync/async choice.

mcqs.question: An Order Service synchronously calls Inventory, Payments, and Shipping in sequence to handle one request, and none of those calls run in parallel. What roughly determines the total latency the original caller experiences?
options: The average latency across all three downstream services
Only the latency of whichever downstream service is called first
The latency of the fastest of the three downstream services
Close to the sum of the sequential calls, dominated by the slowest one if any call blocks the next
mcqs.explanation: When calls happen in sequence rather than in parallel, their latencies add up, and a single slow call in the chain adds directly to the total — not the average or the fastest, and not just the first call in isolation. This is exactly why fan-out latency is closer to a sum (or the slowest link) than an average.

mcqs.question: Two internal services that you fully control on both ends need a high-volume, low-latency channel with a strict, code-generated contract. Which is the better default: REST or gRPC?
options: REST, because JSON is easier for a human to read while debugging
gRPC, because its binary protobuf payloads and generated client/server code favor speed and contract safety for internal service-to-service traffic
REST, because it is the only option that supports streaming
Neither — external partner APIs and internal service calls should always use the same protocol
mcqs.explanation: gRPC's protobuf payloads are smaller and faster to serialize than JSON, and its `.proto`-generated code catches contract mismatches at compile time — exactly what high-volume, fully-internal calls benefit from. REST is easier to read with curl but that matters less for machine-to-machine traffic, gRPC (not REST) has native streaming, and there's no requirement that internal and external APIs share a protocol.

mcqs.question: Service C's database query slows from 20ms to 8 seconds. Service B calls C synchronously with no timeout, and Service A calls B synchronously with no timeout. What is the likely outcome?
options: Only Service C is affected, since A and B are independently healthy services
Service B automatically retries with exponential backoff and the slowdown is absorbed
A and B stay responsive, since synchronous calls do not consume server resources while waiting
Threads or connections in B and then A get tied up waiting, and the slowdown can cascade into a full outage across the chain
mcqs.explanation: Without timeouts, blocked calls hold threads or connections open in every synchronous caller upstream, so C's slowdown can exhaust B's and then A's capacity, cascading into a broader outage. Being individually healthy doesn't protect A and B once they're blocked waiting; nothing here adds automatic retry/backoff; and waiting on a synchronous call does consume resources (a held thread or connection), it isn't free.
